newsitem.title: UK: LME Board to set out proposals to alter its balanc.
newsitem.headline: LME Board to set out proposals to alter its balanc.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) Board meeting on Friday is likely to set out proposals that shift its balance of power, giving more emphasis to the non-ring directorship, trade sources said.
The Board has circulated draft proposals to interested parties for their responses. Sources said that the proposals entail changing the composition of the Board.
If adopted, non-ring dealing members on the Board would be able to out-vote the ring-dealing directors.

If this measure is ratified, then the LME will call a special EGM to be voted on by the wider membership, as this is altering the Exchange's constitution. This meeting will be held in early March, they said.
"This was pretty much on the cards, and it does make sense," one said.
Increasingly now, non-ring dealing companies, such as banks and investment houses, have a greater and more diverse role in the metals business.

Also, last December, the make-up of the board was one of the areas highlighted by the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) in the review of the market it carried out after the Sumitomo Corp copper scandal.
The SIB said there was considerable support for the view that that the Board's composition should better represent the membership as a whole.
At present ring-dealers, provide eight of the sixteen members. Three directors are elected from non-ring members, there are four invited directors, as well as the LME's Chief Executive.

The SIB said many of those consulted for its review attached considerable importance to the need for more directors having no association with the metal industry, which would provide more impartiality.
The current arrangement is seen as favouring ring-members unduly and being out of touch with the wider LME membership.
However, some sources were unhappy with the prospect of such a measure being enabled. The ring-dealers on the LME account for over two-thirds of the Exchange's cleared business.
Also, the 16 ring-dealers have much higher costs to cover in running their operations on the floor.
"It costs a heck of a lot to be a ring-dealing member. We are the market to some extent," one said.
